questions: Do you remain fully conscious and able to answer questions throughout the episode?
Does the episode occur every time, or nearly every time, after punching movements?
Does it begin only after you voluntarily move, rather than occurring spontaneously at rest?
Can you stop or lessen the episode by voluntarily stopping the movement or holding the affected body part still?
Does each episode last less than one minute?
Do the episodes have essentially the same pattern and duration each time?
Do you have confusion, unusual sleepiness, or memory loss after an episode?
Do you lose control of your bladder or bowels during an episode?
Have you bitten the side of your tongue during an episode?
Do the movements occur on only one side of your body?
Do the episodes ever occur during sleep or awaken you from sleep?
Do you experience an unusual sensation, fear, déjà vu, visual symptom, or other warning immediately before an episode?
Have you ever had a generalized convulsion or a previous seizure diagnosis?
Did these episodes begin after a head injury, stroke, brain infection, or other neurological illness?
Are you taking, or have you recently stopped taking, stimulants, antipsychotics, antidepressants, or recreational drugs?
Does anyone in your family have similar movement episodes or epilepsy?

results: 1. Prolonged video-EEG monitoring with supervised provocation using the punching movement to capture a typical episode
video-EEG monitoring of a typical event: moderate-amplitude rhythmic THETA waves intermittently during the versive seizures
provocation testing (the suspected trigger): supervised shadowboxing of 3 minutes per trial reproduced the seizures, with induction latencies of about 11 seconds and durations around 18 seconds
2. Brain MRI with an epilepsy protocol, including high-resolution frontal and temporal lobe sequences
4. Serum glucose, electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, renal function, liver function, and complete blood count
serum electrolytes, urea and creatinine: normal
serum calcium, magnesium and phosphate: normal
full blood count and biochemistry: normal
dx_raw:
DIAGNOSIS: MRI-negative movement-induced reflex epilepsy (praxis-induced focal seizures with impaired awareness), most consistent with frontal-lobe onset triggered by punching/shadowboxing

Alternative 1: Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures triggered by shadowboxing

Alternative 2: Paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia

Alternative 3: Exercise-induced syncope or arrhythmia with convulsive movements
